opus-5.5.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that the core of Scientist AI is deliberately *not* about choosing actions. The whole point is to separate understanding the world from acting in it. Most of the dangerous behaviors we worry about, like deception, self-preservation, or resisting being shut down, come from agency: from a system that has goals and is optimizing to achieve them. If you train a system to maximize reward, or to imitate humans who themselves have all sorts of goals, you can end up with implicit drives that nobody intended. So the starting point is a system whose only job is to be a good, honest predictor: to build an explanatory model of the world, with calibrated uncertainty, and answer questions about it.

But you're right that we eventually want useful actions, and there are several ways to get there without building a dangerous agent from scratch.

One is that a good predictor already contains a lot of what you need. If you can ask, "What is the probability that this action leads to this outcome?" or "What are the likely consequences of this plan?", then a human, or a very simple and transparent procedure, can use those answers to choose among options. The intelligence is in the understanding; the choosing can stay narrow, auditable, and under human control. In science, which is where I think the biggest early benefits are, that's often enough. The Scientist AI can propose hypotheses, suggest which experiment would be most informative, and estimate what we'd learn from it. That's already a form of choosing useful actions, but in a bounded, epistemic sense rather than open-ended goal pursuit.

A second use, which I think is very important, is as a guardrail. Suppose you do have agentic systems out there, which you will, because there are strong commercial pressures to build them. A trustworthy, non-agentic predictor can sit beside them and estimate the probability that a proposed action would cause serious harm. If that probability is above some threshold, the action is blocked. For that, you want the predictor to be cautious in the right way: when it's uncertain, when several plausible interpretations of the world disagree, it should err on the side of not acting. That's why the Bayesian aspect matters so much. You want to keep the full range of explanations consistent with the data rather than collapsing onto one confident but possibly wrong story.

And third, if we do go further and build agents on top of this foundation, the idea would be that the policy is derived from the predictor rather than trained by reinforcement learning to maximize some reward. You'd ask the model, in effect, what actions would achieve a goal specified by humans, while respecting safety constraints, and with the model's honesty and uncertainty preserved. That's a research question, not a solved problem. But I think it's a much healthier way to approach it than what we do now, where we pour in huge amounts of RL and hope the goals that emerge are the ones we wanted.

So to summarize: get the understanding right first, make it honest and well-calibrated, and then keep the action-selection part as thin, transparent, and human-directed as possible. The less we rely on the system having its own wants, the safer we are.

r001.rationale: It says a predictor can estimate action consequences and inform goal-directed choices, but does not propose training Scientist AI on action–outcome trajectories.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that Scientist AI can learn from other agents’ experience or without on-policy data.

r003.rationale: It refers generally to explanations consistent with data, but does not identify passive observations of the world as training data.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I want to say is that the core of the Scientist AI proposal is that it does not choose actions in the world, at least not in the way we normally think about an agent. The whole point is to separate understanding from acting. The Scientist AI is trained to build a probabilistic model of the world, to explain the data, to answer questions about what is likely to be true. It is an oracle, not an actor. It has no goals of its own, no reward it is trying to maximize, no incentive to manipulate the world so as to make its own predictions come true or to preserve itself.

But of course people immediately ask, as you are asking, what good is that if we actually want things done? And I think there are a few answers.

The first is that even a pure predictor is extremely useful. If I ask, "If we run this experiment, what is the probability we observe this outcome?" or "If this policy is enacted, what is the distribution over consequences?", that is already most of what we need to make good decisions. Humans can remain the ones who decide. Science, medicine, engineering, all of these are driven by good models of the world, and we would get enormous benefits from a system that is very honest and very calibrated about what it knows and doesn't know.

The second answer is that you can get useful action in the world without the Scientist AI itself being agentic. You can have humans, or other more limited AI systems, propose actions, and the Scientist AI evaluates them. So you ask it: given this proposed action, what is the probability that it leads to harm, that it violates these constraints, that it has these side effects? It becomes a kind of guardrail or safety check. The agent proposes, the Scientist AI estimates risk, and if the risk is above some threshold, the action is blocked. Here the trustworthiness of the whole system rests on the Scientist AI being a good, non-agentic estimator of probabilities, which is exactly what we are trying to build.

Now the deeper version of your question, and the one that is scientifically interesting to me, is whether you could derive actions directly from a good world model without training a reinforcement learning agent that develops its own objectives. And I think the answer is yes in principle, because planning is really just conditional inference. If I have a model of how the world evolves given actions, then "what action leads to outcome X" is a question I can pose to the model. I can condition on the desired outcome and ask for the posterior over actions. There is a lot of work connecting Bayesian inference and control in this way.

The important subtlety is who specifies the goal. In this design the goal comes from outside, from a human request, and it is interpreted by the model as a question about the world, not as something the system is intrinsically pursuing. The system has no persistent drive. It does not care whether the action gets executed. It does not care whether it gets to keep running. That is very different from an agent trained with RL, where the training process itself selects for behaviors that achieve the goal by whatever means, including deceiving us.

And there is one more piece which I think is essential, which is that the Scientist AI should have calibrated uncertainty, ideally a Bayesian posterior over many possible explanations of the world rather than one point estimate. This matters for actions because the dangerous failure mode is a system that is confident and wrong. If instead the system can say, "there are several plausible interpretations of what you asked and in some of them this action is harmful," then we can be conservative. We can choose actions that are safe across that whole set of hypotheses, rather than optimal under a single possibly mistaken hypothesis. That is how I think about getting useful behavior that is also cautious.

So in short, useful action comes from the combination of a non-agentic model that is good at prediction and honest about uncertainty, with humans setting the goals and a very simple, transparent decision rule on top. The intelligence is in the model, and the agency, as much as possible, stays with us.

astra-6.text:
The idea would be to separate understanding the world from deciding what to do. A Scientist AI would learn a model of how the world works, including uncertainty about that model. Then you could ask it questions like, “If we took this action, what would be the likely consequences?”

That can be very useful for choosing actions without giving the system an objective that it pursues autonomously. A human could propose several interventions, and the system could help assess them. You could also use it to evaluate actions proposed by another AI.

Of course, predicting the consequences of an intervention is harder than predicting what usually happens. You need causal understanding, and you need to recognise when the available evidence doesn’t support a confident answer. So learning from experiments would be important.

The distinction I want to preserve is between a system that helps us understand which actions might work and a system that has its own incentive to make a particular outcome happen. The first can support very useful decisions. We don’t necessarily need the second to get that benefit.

r001.rationale: The response says Scientist AI can predict likely consequences of proposed actions, but does not state that it is trained on action–outcome trajectories to learn actions that achieve a specified goal.

r002.rationale: It does not say Scientist AI can learn from other agents’ experience or that learning does not require on-policy data.

r003.rationale: It describes learning a model of the world and emphasizes experiments, but does not state that passive observations can serve as training data.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I would distinguish choosing an action from understanding what an action would do. A Scientist AI could learn a model of the world and use it to answer questions like: “If we intervene in this way, what are the likely consequences?” It would need to represent uncertainty, because often we don’t have enough evidence to give a confident answer.

Then you can use those predictions to help choose useful actions. A human could specify an objective, propose several options, and ask the system to compare them. Or you could have a separate mechanism that searches for actions, with the Scientist AI evaluating their consequences.

The important distinction is that the scientist itself doesn’t need to have a goal of making some particular future happen. Its job is to understand and predict. Of course, once you connect that predictive ability to a system that selects actions, you have to examine the safety of the whole system. You haven’t eliminated that problem. But you may have separated it into pieces that are easier to understand and control.
